chapter: Returning to the US and the Savoy band
title: Racial situation in Europe versus the United States
summary: Carter found Europeans accepted him as a human being, though he knew what he was returning to.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: Before we go in to the Savoy and the formation of your band, I would like to ask you what your impressions were about the, let's say, the racial situation, aside from the musical situation in the States, or along the East Coast, as contrasted -- if it is contrasted -- with what you had experienced for several years, three years about, in Europe. Did you find, for example, that Europe

Oh yes -- quite definitely. I did. Yes. Of course, I had lived practically all of my life, prior to going to Europe, I had lived in New York, which was maybe a little better than some of the areas below, you know, south of the Mason/Dixon line.

But still, it was a decided difference in the acceptance of you just on the basis of you as a human being, rather than on the basis of the color of your skin. And this, of course, was very nice to find. But when I -- you mean, what was the difference when I returned?

Yeah, was there anything about the racial situation that bothered you, or you know, as a contrast, or were you just absorbed in your music and your professional life taking up the reins again in this country?

Well, I was of course, absorbed in my musical life, and interested in trying to get a band together, but as far as the racial situation was concerned, I knew what I was returning to, so there were no surprises, you know, and I've always been kind of able to live within a situation that I know exists, and at the same time, do everything that I can do to change it. But not to make myself miserable because of it.
But of course, the situation was quite different than it had been in Europe, you know.
